agents.name: Browserbase
agents.purpose_quote: Browserbase is the complete platform to build and deploy agents that browse and interact with the web like humans.
agents.note: Cloud browser sessions run by Browserbase customers' agents; the traffic is driven by the customer, not by Browserbase itself. Sessions present an ordinary browser User-Agent with no Browserbase product token: for Verified sessions, choosing an OS "changes the user agent and browser environment to match the selected platform" (source verified), and the Fetch API is routed "with a real browser User-Agent by default" (source fetch). No IP ranges, reverse DNS rule or ASN are published; sessions can also exit through Browserbase-managed proxies or a customer's own proxy. robots.txt: the docs advise customers to check robots.txt ("Check robots.txt for crawling guidelines when applicable.", best practices on the identity page) but do not say the platform itself enforces it, so the policy is recorded as unstated. The only verifiable identity is Web Bot Auth, which is in beta and enabled per customer account (see signing).

signing.note: Meta's crawler documentation does not mention HTTP message signatures or Web Bot Auth. A third-party survey (mod_pagespeed blog, probe of 19 October 2026) lists this directory, which it took from Cloudflare Radar, and attributes it to a bot it calls Meta-ExternalTest; Meta's own page does not list that bot, so covers is left empty. On 2026-10-26 the URL returned 200 with content type application/http-message-signatures-directory+json and five Ed25519 keys without kid values. https://meta.com/ redirects (301) to the www host; https://www.facebook.com/ returns 404 for the well-known path. The developers.facebook.com page answered 400 to a browser-like User-Agent, 200 HTML to the directory builder's User-Agent and 200 Markdown to curl's default User-Agent; the quotes here use the HTML wording (curly apostrophes), while the Markdown rendering has straight ones.

agents.note: The server-side web_search tool of the xAI API, run when an API caller enables it. The docs do not say what User-Agent, IP addresses or robots.txt policy its page fetches use, so its requests cannot be told apart from other traffic. How the consumer Grok apps (grok.com, iOS, Android) fetch pages is not documented either.

agents.name: Grok Bot
agents.purpose_quote: Each Bot works on a persistent cloud computer with a browser, filesystem, and terminal, so tasks finish in your real tools instead of as chat drafts.
agents.note: xAI's docs give no User-Agent string or token for Grok Bot's browser and say nothing about robots.txt. On sites that resist automation the FAQ says "The Bot should hand those steps to you rather than bypassing them." (source grok-bot-faq). Hosted computers use shared static egress ranges, but these are not published: "Current ranges are available from your account team." (source grok-bot-security-faq). Members can also route a computer's traffic through their own desktop or network, which then shows that network's IP address.

agents.name: grok-agent
agents.purpose_quote: Fetch the content of a specific URL and return it as markdown.
agents.note: The web_fetch tool of the Grok Build coding CLI (xai-org/grok-build). Its source sets the User-Agent to "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; grok-agent/1.0; +https://x.ai)" (USER_AGENT_STRING in config.rs, source grok-build-webfetch-config). The token comes from xAI's own source code, not from a docs page. The tool runs on the user's own machine (or an egress proxy the user sets), so there is no xAI IP range. It is off unless the user turns it on (GROK_WEB_FETCH, "Off by default for security.", source grok-build-settings) and by default only fetches a built-in allowlist of documentation domains. No robots.txt check appears in the web_fetch source files read on 2026-10-26, and no docs page states a robots.txt policy.
